    28	noncomputable section
    29	
    30	/-- The Pauli-test error scale.  The argument order is `(a, b, ε, m, d, q)`;
    31	the powers are real `rpow`s and the asymptotic constants are absorbed into `a`,
    32	as specified by blueprint `thm:pauli`,
    33	paper `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`).
    34	-/
    35	noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
    36	  a * Real.rpow ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) a *
    37	    (Real.rpow ε b + Real.rpow (q : ℝ) (-b) +
    38	      Real.rpow 2 (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))
    39	
    40	/-- Monotonicity obligation for adjusting the universal constants in
    41	`deltaQld` on the source parameter domain. This Lean-only helper supports the
    42	enlargement of `a` and shrinkage of `b` for `0 ≤ ε ≤ 1` recorded in
    43	`rem:pauli-robustness-form` and stated as `lem:delta-qld-mono-support`,
    44	blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex`; the source makes this constant adjustment
    45	at `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1402`. It is
    46	not an additional hypothesis of `thm:pauli` or `lem:qld-4-7`. -/
    47	theorem deltaQld_mono {P : AdmissibleParams} {a a' b b' ε : ℝ}
    48	    (ha0 : 1 ≤ a) (ha : a ≤ a') (hb : b' ≤ b) (hb' : 0 < b')
    49	    (hε0 : 0 ≤ ε) (hε1 : ε ≤ 1) :
    50	    deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ≤ deltaQld a' b' ε P.m P.d P.q := by
    51	  have hmd : (1 : ℝ) ≤ ((P.m * P.d : ℕ) : ℝ) :=
    52	    Nat.one_le_cast.mpr (Nat.mul_pos P.one_le_m P.hd)
    53	  have hmd0 : (0 : ℝ) ≤ ((P.m * P.d : ℕ) : ℝ) := by linarith
    54	  have hq : (1 : ℝ) ≤ (P.q : ℝ) := by
    55	    obtain ⟨k, -, hk⟩ := P.hq
    56	    rw [hk]
    57	    exact_mod_cast Nat.one_le_pow _ _ (by norm_num)
    58	  unfold deltaQld
    59	  simp only [Real.rpow_eq_pow]
    60	  have h1 : ((P.m * P.d : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ a ≤ ((P.m * P.d : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ a' :=
    61	    Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_exponent_le hmd ha
    62	  have h2 : ε ^ b ≤ ε ^ b' := Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_exponent_ge' hε0 hε1 hb'.le hb
    63	  have h3 : (P.q : ℝ) ^ (-b) ≤ (P.q : ℝ) ^ (-b') :=
    64	    Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_exponent_le hq (neg_le_neg hb)
    65	  have h4 : (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b * ((P.m * P.d : ℕ) : ℝ))) ≤
    66	      (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b' * ((P.m * P.d : ℕ) : ℝ))) :=
    67	    Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_exponent_le (by norm_num)
    68	      (neg_le_neg (mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right hb hmd0))
    69	  have hsum : 0 ≤ ε ^ b + (P.q : ℝ) ^ (-b) +
    70	      (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b * ((P.m * P.d : ℕ) : ℝ))) := by
    71	    have := Real.rpow_nonneg hε0 b
    72	    have := Real.rpow_nonneg (Nat.cast_nonneg P.q) (-b)
    73	    have := Real.rpow_nonneg (by norm_num : (0 : ℝ) ≤ 2)
    74	      (-(b * ((P.m * P.d : ℕ) : ℝ)))
    75	    linarith
    76	  exact mul_le_mul (mul_le_mul ha h1 (Real.rpow_nonneg hmd0 a) (by linarith))
    77	    (add_le_add (add_le_add h2 h3) h4) hsum
    78	    (mul_nonneg (by linarith) (Real.rpow_nonneg hmd0 a'))
    79	
    80	/-- The ideal auxiliary state `aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}` in the shuffled register
    81	ordering.  The EPR factor is the concrete `eprState` from blueprint
    82	`def:EPR`; paper
    83	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`).
    84	-/
    85	noncomputable def idealState (P : AdmissibleParams)
    86	    {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
    87	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
    88	    (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')) :
    89	    EuclideanSpace ℂ ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
    90	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) ×
    91	      (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) ℂ).symm
    92	    (fun p =>
    93	      ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (ιA' × ιB') ℂ) aux (p.1.1, p.2.1)) *
    94	        ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P) ℂ)
    95	          (eprState (PauliRegister P)) (p.1.2, p.2.2)))
    96	
    97	/-- The A-side ideal Pauli projector, with identities on the auxiliary and
    98	B-side registers.  This is a concrete matrix form of the operator comparison
    99	in blueprint `thm:pauli`; paper
   100	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`).
   101	-/
   102	noncomputable def pauliProjOnA'' (P : AdmissibleParams)
   103	    {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   104	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB'] (W : PauliKind)
   105	    (u : PauliRegister P) :
   106	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   107	  fun p q =>
   108	    if p.1.1 = q.1.1 ∧ p.2 = q.2 then
   109	      pauliProj W u p.1.2 q.1.2
   110	    else 0
   111	
   112	/-- The symmetric B-side ideal Pauli projector from blueprint
   113	`thm:pauli`, paper origin
   114	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   115	-/
   116	noncomputable def pauliProjOnB'' (P : AdmissibleParams)
   117	    {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   118	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB'] (W : PauliKind)
   119	    (u : PauliRegister P) :
   120	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   121	  fun p q =>
   122	    if p.1 = q.1 ∧ p.2.1 = q.2.1 then
   123	      pauliProj W u p.2.2 q.2.2
   124	    else 0
   125	
   126	/-- Lift a conjugated A-side effect to the full ideal register in blueprint
   127	`thm:pauli`, paper origin
   128	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   129	-/
   130	noncomputable def liftedAEffect {P : AdmissibleParams} {G : Game}
   131	    (S : Strategy G) {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   132	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
   133	    (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   134	      EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P))
   135	    (M : Op S.ιA) :
   136	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   137	  fun p q =>
   138	    if p.2 = q.2 then
   139	      (conjIsometry φA M) p.1 q.1
   140	    else 0
   141	
   142	/-- Lift a conjugated B-side effect to the full ideal register in blueprint
   143	`thm:pauli`, paper origin
   144	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   145	-/
   146	noncomputable def liftedBEffect {P : AdmissibleParams} {G : Game}
   147	    (S : Strategy G) {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   148	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
   149	    (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   150	      EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
   151	    (M : Op S.ιB) :
   152	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   153	  fun p q =>
   154	    if p.1 = q.1 then
   155	      (conjIsometry φB M) p.2 q.2
   156	    else 0
   157	
   158	/-- A finite witness packaging the auxiliary dimensions, isometries, and state
   159	from `thm:pauli`.  This structure is a Lean-only encoding of the existential
   160	data in the paper theorem; it introduces no extra hypothesis.  Blueprint
   161	`thm:pauli`, paper origin
   162	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   163	-/
   164	structure PauliSoundnessWitness (P : AdmissibleParams)
   165	    (S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P)) where
   166	  ιA' : Type
   167	  ιB' : Type
   168	  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA']
   169	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB']
   170	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA']
   171	  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB']
   172	  φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   173	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P)
   174	  φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   175	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P)
   176	  aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')

   179	attribute [instance] PauliSoundnessWitness.ιAFintype PauliSoundnessWitness.ιBFintype

   181	
   182	/-- The A-side operator-distance quantity appearing in the soundness

    92	    DirectLdSpace D ≃
    93	      (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) ×
    94	        (Fin D.m × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) where
    95	  toFun sample := (sample.point, sample.index, sample.direction)
    96	  invFun sample := ⟨sample.1, sample.2.1, sample.2.2⟩
    97	  left_inv sample := by cases sample; rfl
    98	  right_inv sample := by cases sample; rfl
    99	
   100	/-- Decompose a direct sample into its stored index and the remaining
   101	independent coordinates. -/
   102	def directLdSpaceIndexEquiv (D : DirectLdParams) :
   103	    DirectLdSpace D ≃
   104	      Fin D.m ×
   105	        ((Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) ×
   106	          (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) where
   107	  toFun sample := (sample.index, sample.point, sample.direction)
   108	  invFun sample := ⟨sample.2.1, sample.1, sample.2.2⟩
   109	  left_inv sample := by cases sample; rfl
   110	  right_inv sample := by cases sample; rfl
   111	
   112	/-- Compatibility name for the index-first direct-sample decomposition. -/
   113	abbrev directLdSpaceIndexSplitEquiv (D : DirectLdParams) :
   114	    DirectLdSpace D ≃
   115	      Fin D.m × ((Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :=
   116	  directLdSpaceIndexEquiv D
   117	
   118	/-- Zero the coordinates preceding the directly sampled prefix index. -/
   119	def directPrefixProjection {D : DirectLdParams} (i : Fin D.m)
   120	    (v : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D :=
   121	  fun j => if j.val < i.val then 0 else v j
   122	
   123	/-- Zeroing the coordinates preceding a prefix index is idempotent: the
   124	coordinates it leaves unchanged are exactly those it does not zero. -/
   125	theorem directPrefixProjection_idem (D : DirectLdParams) (i : Fin D.m)
   126	    (v : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) :
   127	    directPrefixProjection i (directPrefixProjection i v) =
   128	      directPrefixProjection i v := by
   129	  funext j
   130	  unfold directPrefixProjection
   131	  split_ifs <;> rfl

   133	/-- Canonical line descriptions whose coordinate index is stored directly.
   134	Coordinates are numbered from zero, so `index = i` represents coordinate
   135	`i + 1` in the paper. -/
   136	inductive DirectLineDesc (D : DirectLdParams) where
   137	  | axis (base : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) (index : Fin D.m)
   138	      (baseFixed : lineRepMap (coordinateDirection index) base = base)
   139	  | diagonal (base : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) (index : Fin D.m)
   140	      (direction : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)
   141	      (baseFixed : lineRepMap direction base = base)
   142	      (prefixZero : ∀ j : Fin D.m, j.val < index.val → direction j = 0)
   143	  deriving DecidableEq

   145	/-! ## Finite direct-line carrier -/
   146	
   147	/-- A finite code for directly indexed lines, omitting only proof fields. -/
   148	private abbrev DirectLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :=
   149	  ((Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m) ⊕
   150	    ((Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m ×
   151	      (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D))
   152	
   153	/-- Encode a directly indexed line by its tag and mathematical data. -/
   154	private def directLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :
   155	    DirectLineDesc D → DirectLineDescCode D
   156	  | .axis base index _ => .inl (base, index)
   157	  | .diagonal base index direction _ _ => .inr (base, index, direction)
   158	
   159	/-- The direct-line code is injective by proof irrelevance. -/
   160	private theorem directLineDescCode_injective (D : DirectLdParams) :
   161	    Function.Injective (directLineDescCode D) := by
   162	  intro line line' h
   163	  cases line with
   164	  | axis base index baseFixed =>
   165	      cases line' with
   166	      | axis base' index' baseFixed' =>
   167	          simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inl.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
   168	          rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
   169	          rfl
   170	      | diagonal => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
   171	  | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero =>
   172	      cases line' with
   173	      | axis => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
   174	      | diagonal base' index' direction' baseFixed' prefixZero' =>
   175	          simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inr.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
   176	          rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl, rfl⟩
   177	          rfl
   178	
   179	/-- Directly indexed line descriptions form a finite type. -/
   180	noncomputable instance directLineDescFintype (D : DirectLdParams) :
   181	    Fintype (DirectLineDesc D) :=
   182	  Fintype.ofInjective (directLineDescCode D) (directLineDescCode_injective D)
   183	
   184	/-- The kind of a directly indexed line. -/
   185	def DirectLineDesc.kind {D : DirectLdParams} : DirectLineDesc D → LineKind
   186	  | .axis _ _ _ => .axis
   187	  | .diagonal _ _ _ _ _ => .diagonal
   188	
   189	/-- The coordinate index stored in a directly indexed line. -/
   190	def DirectLineDesc.index {D : DirectLdParams} : DirectLineDesc D → Fin D.m
   191	  | .axis _ index _ => index
   192	  | .diagonal _ index _ _ _ => index
   193	
   194	/-- The canonical base point of a directly indexed line. -/
   195	def DirectLineDesc.base {D : DirectLdParams} :
   196	    DirectLineDesc D → Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D
   197	  | .axis base _ _ => base
   198	  | .diagonal base _ _ _ _ => base
   199	
   200	/-- The geometric direction of a directly indexed line. -/
   201	def DirectLineDesc.direction {D : DirectLdParams} (line : DirectLineDesc D) :
   202	    Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D :=
   203	  match line with
   204	  | .axis _ index _ => coordinateDirection index
   205	  | .diagonal _ _ direction _ _ => direction
   206	
   207	/-- The base of a directly indexed description is fixed by its geometric
   208	direction. -/
   209	theorem DirectLineDesc.base_fixed {D : DirectLdParams} (line : DirectLineDesc D) :
   210	    lineRepMap line.direction line.base = line.base := by
   211	  cases line with
   212	  | axis base index baseFixed => exact baseFixed
   213	  | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero => exact baseFixed
   214	
   215	/-- Every directly indexed diagonal description retains its prefix-zero
   216	invariant. -/
   217	theorem DirectLineDesc.diagonal_prefix_zero {D : DirectLdParams}
   218	    (line : DirectLineDesc D) (hline : line.kind = .diagonal) :
   219	    ∀ j : Fin D.m, j.val < line.index.val → line.direction j = 0 := by
   220	  cases line with
   221	  | axis base index baseFixed => simp [DirectLineDesc.kind] at hline
   222	  | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero => exact prefixZero
   223	
   224	/-- The point set represented by a directly indexed line. -/
   225	noncomputable def DirectLineDesc.pointSet {D : DirectLdParams}
   226	    (line : DirectLineDesc D) : Set (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) :=
   227	  linePoints line.base line.direction
   228	
   229	/-- Turn a direct sample into its canonical axis-line description. -/
   230	noncomputable def directALineDescOf (D : DirectLdParams)
   231	    (sample : DirectLdSpace D) : DirectLineDesc D :=
   232	  let direction := coordinateDirection sample.index
   233	  let base := lineRepMap direction sample.point
   234	  .axis base sample.index (lineRepMap_apply_self direction sample.point)
   235	
   236	/-- Turn a direct sample into its canonical diagonal-line description. -/
   237	noncomputable def directDLineDescOf (D : DirectLdParams)
   238	    (sample : DirectLdSpace D) : DirectLineDesc D :=
   239	  let direction := directPrefixProjection sample.index sample.direction
   240	  let base := lineRepMap direction sample.point
   241	  .diagonal base sample.index direction
   242	    (lineRepMap_apply_self direction sample.point) (by
   243	      intro j hj
   244	      change directPrefixProjection sample.index sample.direction j = 0
   245	      rw [directPrefixProjection, if_pos hj])
   246	
   247	/-- The axis-line/point law with a directly sampled coordinate index. -/
   248	noncomputable def directALinePointDist (D : DirectLdParams) :
   249	    Distribution (DirectLineDesc D × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :=
   250	  (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D)).map fun sample =>
   251	    (directALineDescOf D sample, sample.point)
   252	
   253	/-- The diagonal-line/point law with a directly sampled prefix index. -/
   254	noncomputable def directDLinePointDist (D : DirectLdParams) :
   255	    Distribution (DirectLineDesc D × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :=
   256	  (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D)).map fun sample =>
   257	    (directDLineDescOf D sample, sample.point)
   258	
   259	/-- The equal mixture of the directly indexed axis and diagonal line-point
   260	laws.  This is the replacement for the otherwise undefined extended-dimension
   261	instance used at paper
   262	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1020-1116`. -/
   263	noncomputable def directLinePointDist (D : DirectLdParams) :
   264	    Distribution (DirectLineDesc D × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :=
   265	  Distribution.mix (1 / 2) (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
   266	    (directALinePointDist D) (directDLinePointDist D)
   267	
   268	/-- The directly indexed axis-line/point law is probabilistic. -/
   269	theorem directALinePointDist_isProbability (D : DirectLdParams) :
   270	    (directALinePointDist D).IsProbability := by
   271	  exact (uniformDistribution_isProbability (DirectLdSpace D)).map _
   272	
   273	/-- The directly indexed diagonal-line/point law is probabilistic. -/
   274	theorem directDLinePointDist_isProbability (D : DirectLdParams) :
   275	    (directDLinePointDist D).IsProbability := by
   276	  exact (uniformDistribution_isProbability (DirectLdSpace D)).map _
   277	
   278	/-- The directly indexed line-point mixture is probabilistic. -/
   279	theorem directLinePointDist_isProbability (D : DirectLdParams) :
   280	    (directLinePointDist D).IsProbability := by
   281	  exact Distribution.mix_isProbability _ _ _
   282	    (directALinePointDist_isProbability D) (directDLinePointDist_isProbability D)
   283	    (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
   284	
   285	/-- The point and stored-index marginals of the direct axis-line law are
   286	uniform.  This is a direct-index analogue of `lem:alnf`, required by
   287	the repair described in `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`;
   288	the source distribution is at
   289	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:243-257`.

   291	theorem directALinePointDist_point_index_marginal_uniform (D : DirectLdParams) :
   292	    (directALinePointDist D).map Prod.snd =
   293	        uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) ∧
   294	      (directALinePointDist D).map (fun sample => sample.1.index) =
   295	        uniformDistribution (Fin D.m) := by
   296	  constructor
   297	  · unfold directALinePointDist
   298	    rw [Distribution.map_map]
   299	    simpa [Function.comp_def] using
   300	      (uniformDistribution_map_fst_of_equiv
   301	        (e := directLdSpacePointEquiv D)
   302	        (f := fun sample : DirectLdSpace D => sample.point) (by intro; rfl))
   303	  · unfold directALinePointDist
   304	    rw [Distribution.map_map]
   305	    simpa [Function.comp_def, directALineDescOf, DirectLineDesc.index] using
   306	      (uniformDistribution_map_fst_of_equiv
   307	        (e := directLdSpaceIndexEquiv D)
   308	        (f := fun sample : DirectLdSpace D => sample.index) (by intro; rfl))
   309	
   310	/-- Every sampled direct axis line contains its paired point.  This is the
   311	Direct-index incidence obligation corresponding to `lem:alnf` and
   312	the repair in `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`. -/
   313	theorem directALinePointDist_mem_line (D : DirectLdParams) :
   314	    ∀ sample ∈ (directALinePointDist D).support,
   315	      sample.2 ∈ sample.1.pointSet := by
   316	  intro sample hsample
   317	  rw [directALinePointDist, Distribution.map_support,
   318	    uniformDistribution_support] at hsample
   319	  rcases Finset.mem_image.mp hsample with ⟨source, _, rfl⟩
   320	  simpa [directALineDescOf, DirectLineDesc.pointSet,
   321	    DirectLineDesc.base, DirectLineDesc.direction] using
   322	    (mem_linePoints_lineRepMap
   323	      (coordinateDirection source.index) source.point)

   330	    (directDLinePointDist D).map Prod.snd =
   331	        uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) ∧
   332	      (directDLinePointDist D).map (fun sample => sample.1.index) =
   333	        uniformDistribution (Fin D.m) := by
   334	  constructor
   335	  · unfold directDLinePointDist
   336	    rw [Distribution.map_map]
   337	    simpa [Function.comp_def] using

   339	        (e := directLdSpacePointEquiv D)
   340	        (f := fun sample : DirectLdSpace D => sample.point) (by intro; rfl))
   341	  · unfold directDLinePointDist
   342	    rw [Distribution.map_map]
   343	    simpa [Function.comp_def, directDLineDescOf, DirectLineDesc.index] using
   344	      (uniformDistribution_map_fst_of_equiv
   345	        (e := directLdSpaceIndexEquiv D)
   346	        (f := fun sample : DirectLdSpace D => sample.index) (by intro; rfl))

   348	/-- Every sampled direct diagonal line contains its paired point.  This is the
   349	Direct-index incidence obligation corresponding to `lem:dlnf`. -/
   350	theorem directDLinePointDist_mem_line (D : DirectLdParams) :
   351	    ∀ sample ∈ (directDLinePointDist D).support,

   353	  intro sample hsample

   364	`lem:dlnf`, paper
   365	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:261-272`.

     7	/-!
     8	# A uniform point of the extended space from the sub-line law
     9	
    10	The first scalar estimate in the combining argument samples an extended line
    11	from the sub-line witness and then a uniform affine parameter on that line.
    12	This module records that the resulting extended point is uniform and hence
    13	that its two source coordinate blocks are independent uniform points.
    14	
    15	## References
    16	
    17	These statements support `lem:claim-17-1` in
    18	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex`.  The paper uses this sampling
    19	fact at
    20	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1159-1166`.
    21	-/

    31	/-- If every slice of a map of a pair carries the second uniform law to one
    32	fixed law, then the map carries the uniform law of the pair to that law. -/
    33	theorem uniformDistribution_map_uncurry {α β γ : Type*}
    34	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α]
    35	    [Fintype β] [DecidableEq β] [Nonempty β] [DecidableEq γ]
    36	    (g : α × β → γ) (ν : Distribution γ)
    37	    (hg : ∀ a, (uniformDistribution β).map (fun b => g (a, b)) = ν) :
    38	    (uniformDistribution (α × β)).map g = ν := by
    39	  rw [← bind_uniformDistribution_map (fun a b => g (a, b)),
    40	    show (fun a => (uniformDistribution β).map (fun b => g (a, b))) =
    41	      fun _ => ν from funext hg]
    42	  exact Distribution.bind_const _ (uniformDistribution_isProbability α) ν
    43	
    44	/-- Reading a point at a uniform affine parameter on the canonical line of a
    45	uniform direct sample gives a uniform point of the direct coordinate space. -/
    46	theorem uniformDistribution_map_directLine_add_smul (D : DirectLdParams)
    47	    (V : Fin D.m × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) → (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :
    48	    (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D × DirectScalarQ D)).map
    49	        (fun p => lineRepMap (V (p.1.index, p.1.direction)) p.1.point +
    50	          p.2 • V (p.1.index, p.1.direction)) =
    51	      uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) := by
    52	  classical
    53	  let e : DirectLdSpace D × DirectScalarQ D ≃
    54	      (Fin D.m × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) ×
    55	        ((Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) × DirectScalarQ D) :=
    56	    { toFun := fun p => ((p.1.index, p.1.direction), (p.1.point, p.2))
    57	      invFun := fun w => (⟨w.2.1, w.1.1, w.1.2⟩, w.2.2)
    58	      left_inv := by rintro ⟨⟨pt, i, dir⟩, t⟩; rfl
    59	      right_inv := by rintro ⟨⟨i, dir⟩, pt, t⟩; rfl }
    60	  have hequiv :
    61	      (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D × DirectScalarQ D)).map e =
    62	        uniformDistribution ((Fin D.m × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) ×
    63	          ((Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) × DirectScalarQ D)) :=
    64	    uniformDistribution_map_equiv e
    65	  have hmap :
    66	      (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D × DirectScalarQ D)).map
    67	          (fun p => lineRepMap (V (p.1.index, p.1.direction)) p.1.point +
    68	            p.2 • V (p.1.index, p.1.direction)) =
    69	        ((uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D × DirectScalarQ D)).map e).map
    70	          (fun w => lineRepMap (V w.1) w.2.1 + w.2.2 • V w.1) := by
    71	    rw [Distribution.map_map]
    72	    rfl
    73	  rw [hmap, hequiv]
    74	  refine uniformDistribution_map_uncurry _ _ fun a => ?_
    75	  exact uniformDistribution_map_lineRepMap_add_smul (V a)

    77	/-- Averaging a function at a uniform affine parameter on the canonical line
    78	of a uniform direct sample is averaging it at a uniform point. -/
    79	theorem avgOver_uniform_directLdSpace_line_add_smul (D : DirectLdParams)
    80	    (V : Fin D.m × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) → (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D))
    81	    (g : (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) → ℝ) :
    82	    avgOver (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D)) (fun s =>
    83	        avgOver (uniformDistribution (DirectScalarQ D)) (fun t =>
    84	          g (lineRepMap (V (s.index, s.direction)) s.point +
    85	            t • V (s.index, s.direction)))) =
    86	      avgOver (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) g := by
    87	  classical
    88	  rw [← avgOver_uniform_prod]
    89	  calc
    90	    avgOver (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D × DirectScalarQ D))
    91	          (fun p => g (lineRepMap (V (p.1.index, p.1.direction)) p.1.point +
    92	            p.2 • V (p.1.index, p.1.direction))) =
    93	        avgOver ((uniformDistribution
    94	            (DirectLdSpace D × DirectScalarQ D)).map
    95	          (fun p => lineRepMap (V (p.1.index, p.1.direction)) p.1.point +
    96	            p.2 • V (p.1.index, p.1.direction))) g :=
    97	      (Distribution.avgOver_map _ _ g).symm
    98	    _ = avgOver (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) g := by
    99	      rw [uniformDistribution_map_directLine_add_smul]

   101	/-- A uniform point on a line drawn from the directly indexed line-point law
   102	is uniform in the ambient coordinate space. -/
   103	theorem avgOver_directLinePointDist_line_add_smul (D : DirectLdParams)
   104	    (g : (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) → ℝ) :
   105	    avgOver ((directLinePointDist D).map Prod.fst) (fun line =>
   106	        avgOver (uniformDistribution (DirectScalarQ D)) (fun t =>
   107	          g (line.base + t • line.direction))) =
   108	      avgOver (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) g := by
   109	  classical
   110	  have haxis :
   111	      avgOver (directALinePointDist D) (fun sample =>
   112	          avgOver (uniformDistribution (DirectScalarQ D)) (fun t =>
   113	            g (sample.1.base + t • sample.1.direction))) =
   114	        avgOver (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) g := by
   115	    rw [directALinePointDist, Distribution.avgOver_map]
   116	    exact avgOver_uniform_directLdSpace_line_add_smul D
   117	      (fun w => coordinateDirection w.1) g
   118	  have hdiag :
   119	      avgOver (directDLinePointDist D) (fun sample =>
   120	          avgOver (uniformDistribution (DirectScalarQ D)) (fun t =>
   121	            g (sample.1.base + t • sample.1.direction))) =
   122	        avgOver (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) g := by
   123	    rw [directDLinePointDist, Distribution.avgOver_map]
   124	    exact avgOver_uniform_directLdSpace_line_add_smul D
   125	      (fun w => directPrefixProjection w.1 w.2) g
   126	  rw [Distribution.avgOver_map, directLinePointDist,
   127	    WinImplications.avgOver_mix, haxis, hdiag]

   130	/-- Identify the directly indexed extended coordinates with the combining
   131	coordinate split. -/
   132	private def extendedFinCombineEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   133	    Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m ≃ ((Fin P.m ⊕ Fin P.m) ⊕ Fin 2) :=
   134	  (finCongr (by rfl)).trans (finCombineEquiv P.m)
   135	
   136	/-- Split an extended point into its two source blocks and two remaining
   137	scalar coordinates. -/
   138	private noncomputable def extendedPointBlocksEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   139	    (Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd) ≃
   140	      ((Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) × (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)) ×
   141	        (Fin 2 → PauliScalar P) :=
   142	  (Equiv.arrowCongr (extendedFinCombineEquiv P)
   143	      (extendedDirectScalarEquiv P)).trans
   144	    ((Equiv.sumArrowEquivProdArrow (Fin P.m ⊕ Fin P.m) (Fin 2)

1	# Lean Proof Integrity Rules
     2	
     3	This file is the **single source of truth** for proof integrity checks in this
     4	repository. All CI workflows and review prompts should reference this file
     5	rather than duplicating the rules inline.
     6	
     7	> **Lean version**: 4.x (Lean 3 keywords like `constant` do not apply)
     8	
     9	> **Companion document:** [`anti_patterns.md`](./anti_patterns.md) catalogues
    10	> subtler proof-evasion patterns that pass every blocker check below yet still
    11	> fail to prove the claimed mathematics (conclusion-shaped hypotheses,
    12	> definitional sleight-of-hand, zero-fallback branches, trivial default
    13	> witnesses, Mathlib-bypass castles, external `*Statement` smuggles).
    14	> Consult it alongside this file during review.
    15	
    16	> **Paper-realignment exception:** When a PR is explicitly realigning a
    17	> source-labelled declaration with `references/ldt-paper/`, the `sorry`
    18	> blocker below may be temporarily relaxed for the affected proof bodies.  The
    19	> PR must restore the source-faithful public statement, name the remaining proof
    20	> obligation as a theorem or lemma, and cite the paper passage plus the
    21	> tracking issue or paper-gap note.  A theorem whose proof still depends on a
    22	> known non-paper bridge, residual, repair input, obligation structure, or
    23	> conditional helper
    24	> must carry the `**Unfaithful:**` docstring marker described in `AGENTS.md`.
    25	> Review such PRs against statement faithfulness and the documented discharge
    26	> plan, not merely against the temporary `sorry` count.
    27	
    28	---
    29	
    30	## Blockers
    31	
    32	These patterns **must** be resolved before merging.
    33	
    34	### Direct proof holes
    35	
    36	| Pattern | Risk |
    37	|---------|------|
    38	| `sorry` | Axiomatically closes any goal — the proof is incomplete |
    39	| `admit` | Tactic alias for `sorry` |
    40	
    41	### Kernel / type system bypasses
    42	
    43	| Pattern | Risk |
    44	|---------|------|
    45	| `native_decide` | Relies on trusted native evaluation / compiler; banned in Mathlib for soundness and process reasons |
    46	| `unsafeCast`, `unsafeCoerce` | Type system bypass — can fabricate any proof term |
    47	| `lcProof` | Low-level proof fabrication primitive — can prove `False` |
    48	| `ofReduceBool`, `ofReduceNat` | Kernel reduction primitives exploitable for unsound proofs |
    49	
    50	### Axiom smuggling
    51	
    52	| Pattern | Risk |
    53	|---------|------|
    54	| `axiom` declarations | Introduces unproven assumptions that could be inconsistent; must be explicitly justified |
    55	
    56	When an external mathematical result must remain unformalized temporarily,
    57	prefer a caller-supplied `Prop` hypothesis over a global `axiom`
    58	declaration, and add a regression check (for example a
    59	`Lean.collectAxioms`-based assertion, as in
    60	`MIPStarRE.LDT.Test.AxiomAudit`) so later refactors cannot silently widen
    61	the axiomatic base.
    62	
    63	This preference does not license proposition inputs on source-labelled paper
    64	theorems.  If the cited paper theorem does not assume the proposition, a
    65	caller-supplied `Prop` hypothesis is an additional theorem hypothesis, not a
    66	proof of the paper statement.  Use such hypotheses only for explicitly
    67	conditional auxiliary results, and keep the source-labelled theorem statement
    68	faithful to the paper.
    69	
    70	### Circular reasoning
    71	
    72	Lean's kernel forbids literal declaration cycles, so focus on **mathematical
    73	circularity**:
    74	
    75	- Proofs that assume (or trivially reintroduce) the statement being proved as a
    76	  local hypothesis, then immediately close the goal from that hypothesis
    77	- Helper lemmas in the same file that essentially restate the main goal and are
    78	  only used to prove that goal
    79	- Local `have`/`let` bindings that are just the goal rephrased, used to solve
    80	  the goal without any real argument
    81	- Newly introduced `axiom` that makes a difficult statement trivially provable
    82	  without connecting to existing Mathlib / core theorems
    83	- Abuse of `unsafe` features to fabricate proofs instead of giving a genuine
    84	  derivation
    85	- `by exact h` where `h` came from an unjustified assumption identical to the
    86	  goal
    87	
    88	### Castle-in-the-air (ungrounded proofs)
    89	
    90	Proofs that avoid grounding in Mathlib:
    91	
    92	- Custom re-declarations of standard Mathlib lemmas (e.g., re-proving
    93	  `add_comm` instead of importing it)
    94	- `axiom` or `sorry`-based helper lemmas for facts that already exist in
    95	  Mathlib
    96	- Chains of custom lemmas that never bottom out in Mathlib or Lean core
    97	- `private` helper lemmas that duplicate Mathlib API (e.g., custom matrix
    98	  transpose lemmas when `Matrix.transpose_*` exists)
    99	- Overly long proof chains replaceable by a single Mathlib lemma
   100	
   101	When flagging, perform an actual lookup (grep, `#find?`, `exact?`,
   102	`library_search`). If an equivalent exists, cite the Mathlib lemma and module
   103	path. If not, state "no equivalent found" with search evidence.
   104	
   105	### Scaffolding that blocks real formalization
   106	
   107	This is a subtle but critical failure mode: **scaffolding definitions or
   108	theorem statements that do not faithfully represent the actual mathematics**,
   109	making them impossible to connect to real Mathlib-based proofs.
   110	
   111	Signs to watch for:
   112	
   113	- Custom type definitions for objects that already exist in Mathlib (e.g.,
   114	  defining a custom `Measurement` type instead of using Mathlib's
   115	  `MeasureTheory` or operator algebra API)
   116	- Theorem statements whose hypotheses or conclusions use project-local types
   117	  that are not definitionally equal to or coercible from the Mathlib versions
   118	- Scaffolded definitions that compile but encode the wrong mathematical
   119	  semantics (e.g., a "projective measurement" definition that does not enforce
   120	  the correct positivity or completeness conditions)
   121	- Intermediate lemmas stated in terms of scaffolding types that cannot be
   122	  connected upstream to Mathlib's API without reproving everything
   123	- Definitions that "work" for `sorry`-based proofs but fail when you try to
   124	  fill in real proofs using Mathlib lemmas (type mismatches, missing instances,
   125	  incompatible universes)
   126	
   127	When reviewing scaffolded code, ask: **Can a real proof be built on top of
   128	this?** If the types, instances, and API surface don't align with Mathlib, the
   129	scaffolding is actively harmful — it creates technical debt that blocks
   130	progress rather than enabling it.
   131	
   132	### Paper-labelled theorem statement drift
   133	
   134	A theorem advertised as the Lean formalization of a paper theorem is a blocker
   135	if its public statement has drifted from the cited paper statement.
   136	Changing a theorem away from the statement in `references/ldt-paper/` is
   137	strongly discouraged unless it is forced by faithful formal encoding or by a
   138	documented mathematical necessity.
   139	
   140	The most common failure mode is replacing an unformalized proof step by an
   141	extra hypothesis on the theorem itself.  This produces a true conditional
   142	theorem, but it is not the theorem stated in the paper.  In particular, do not
   143	repair a theorem such as `mainFormal` by adding assumptions named
   144	`BridgeHypotheses`, `Input`, `Residual`, `Package`, `RepairInput`, `Producer`,
   145	generic `Hypotheses` or `Assumptions` bundles, or similar, unless those
   146	assumptions are explicitly present in the cited paper statement.
   147	
   148	Conditional helpers are a last-resort quarantine for proof work that cannot yet
   149	be closed.  Before introducing one, state the missing intermediate fact as a
   150	named lemma or theorem to be proved from the paper hypotheses.  A conditional
   151	helper is permitted only when it has a paper-gap note or tracking issue, a named
   152	obligation-discharger target, and an explicit removal plan.  Its name must show
   153	that it is conditional, for example with `_of_...`, `_assuming_...`, or
   154	`conditional...`.  It must not be the declaration used by a source-labelled
   155	blueprint theorem with `\leanok`.
   156	
   157	Existing bridge hypotheses should be treated as proof debt.  Mine their proofs
   158	for reusable arguments, but do not keep a paper-labelled theorem in a
   159	strengthened form merely because the conditional version compiles.  If the
   160	bridge data cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the correct repair is
   161	to restore the paper-aligned theorem statement and leave the missing proof as a
   162	tracked `sorry`, rather than to keep the extra assumption on the theorem.

   164	Not every explicit Lean hypothesis is statement drift.  Side conditions needed
   165	to encode the paper's domain, such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model
   166	instances, positivity of parameters, or denominator nonvanishing, may be
   167	faithful when the paper uses the corresponding objects without comment.  These
   168	conditions should still be reviewed.  The issue is whether the hypothesis is
   169	mathematical domain data implicit in the source, or an unproved intermediate
   170	step of the source proof.

   606	## CI prevention
   607	
   608	Mechanical detection is possible for many of these patterns:
   609	
   610	- **A1 (conclusion-shaped hypothesis).** Use
   611	  `python3 scripts/audit_conclusion_shaped_hypotheses.py --ci` as the current
   612	  report-only tripwire for the PR [#491] inline-existential mutation. It parses
   613	  theorem/lemma headers and warns when an explicit existential hypothesis shares
   614	  the conclusion's salient structure, while printing witness-adapter helpers
   615	  separately. When [#438] lands (`\leanok` ↔ `sorryAx` drift), extend the same
   616	  idea to all `\leanok`-tagged declarations: parse the hypothesis list; if any
   617	  hypothesis's type (modulo `∃`/`∀`/`∧`) contains a prefix of the conclusion
   618	  structure, warn.
   619	- **A2 (definitional sleight).** Grep for `theorem <Name>.* := rfl` where
   620	  `<Name>` has a blueprint `\lean{}` cross-reference. The only allowed cases
   621	  are ones annotated with `@[paper_bookkeeping]` (proposed attribute) or in
   622	  an allow-list.
   623	- **A3 (zero-fallback).** Grep for identifier suffixes `fallback`, `or0`,
   624	  `orDefault`, `placeholder`, `sentinel` in `Defs/*` files. Each should have
   625	  a docstring citing the downstream eligibility precondition.
   626	- **A4 (default witnesses).** Grep `:= default`, `refine ⟨default`, `exact
   627	  ⟨default`, `Classical.arbitrary` inside proof bodies (not typeclass
   628	  definitions). Cross-reference to [#1379]'s witness ledger.
   629	- **A5 (Mathlib bypass).** No reliable CI check, but `audits/` reports
   630	  catch it during per-chapter audits.
   631	- **A6 (external smuggles).** Every new `structure *Statement` without a
   632	  producing theorem should be required to carry a `/-- Grounded by: #NNN
   633	  -/` docstring, enforced by a lint rule over `blueprint/`.
   634	
   635	The scripts in `scripts/` (notably `scripts/blueprint_lean_sync.py` and
   636	`scripts/blueprint_leanok_axioms.py`) are the natural home for extensions that
   637	add these checks.
   638

   283	    (a0 : G.AnswerA) (b0 : G.AnswerB) :
   284	    (paddedProjectiveStrategy S a0 b0).value = S.value :=

   293	/-- Every finite tensor-product strategy has an equal-value projective
   294	dilation whose state is obtained by local zero padding. This is
   295	blueprint
   296	`lem:projective-strategy-setup`, paper
   297	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:155-172`.
   298	The proof route is Naimark dilation followed by residual-projector completion. -/
   299	theorem exists_projective_padded_strategy (G : Game) (S : Strategy G) :
   300	    ∃ (nA nB : ℕ) (T : Strategy G)
   301	      (eA : T.ιA ≃ S.ιA × (Fin nA → Bool))
   302	      (eB : T.ιB ≃ S.ιB × (Fin nB → Bool)),
   303	      T.IsProjective ∧
   304	        reindexState (paddedProdShuffle eA eB) T.ψ =
   305	          reindexState (paddedProdShuffle eA eB)
   306	            (isometryTensor (padWithZeros eA) (padWithZeros eB) S.ψ) ∧
   307	        T.value = S.value := by
   308	  classical
   309	  have hlocal := nonempty_of_unit_vector S.ψ S.ψ_norm
   310	  letI : Nonempty S.ιA := hlocal.map Prod.fst
   311	  letI : Nonempty S.ιB := hlocal.map Prod.snd
   312	  have hquestions := nonempty_of_probability G.μ G.μ_prob
   313	  have ha := measurement_outcome_nonempty (S.A hquestions.some.1)
   314	  have hb := measurement_outcome_nonempty (S.B hquestions.some.2)
   315	  let a0 : G.AnswerA := Classical.choice ha
   316	  let b0 : G.AnswerB := Classical.choice hb
   317	  let T : Strategy G := paddedProjectiveStrategy S a0 b0
   318	  let eA : T.ιA ≃ S.ιA ×
   319	      (Fin (Fintype.card G.AnswerA + 1) → Bool) := Equiv.refl _
   320	  let eB : T.ιB ≃ S.ιB ×
   321	      (Fin (Fintype.card G.AnswerB + 1) → Bool) := Equiv.refl _
   322	  refine ⟨Fintype.card G.AnswerA + 1, Fintype.card G.AnswerB + 1,
   323	    T, eA, eB, paddedProjectiveStrategy_isProjective S a0 b0, ?_,
   324	    paddedProjectiveStrategy_value S a0 b0⟩
   325	  apply congrArg (reindexState (paddedProdShuffle eA eB))
   326	  change padState (0 : Fin (Fintype.card G.AnswerA + 1) → Bool)
   327	      (0 : Fin (Fintype.card G.AnswerB + 1) → Bool) S.ψ =
   328	    isometryTensor
   329	      (padWithZeros (Equiv.refl (S.ιA ×
   330	        (Fin (Fintype.card G.AnswerA + 1) → Bool))))
   331	      (padWithZeros (Equiv.refl (S.ιB ×
   332	        (Fin (Fintype.card G.AnswerB + 1) → Bool)))) S.ψ
   333	  exact (isometryTensor_padWithZeros_refl S.ψ).symm

     6	This module records the unit upper bound for the pointwise consistency defect

    25	/-- The pointwise defect of complete measurements on opposite registers is at
    26	most one: it equals one minus a nonnegative diagonal overlap. This proof-only
    27	bound restores discarded mass graded by the ambient line-point distribution. -/
    28	theorem consistencyDefect_integrand_le_one {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε : ℝ}
    29	    {Outcome : Type*} [Fintype Outcome] [DecidableEq Outcome]
    30	    (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (p1 p2 : Placement) (hopp : p1.IsOpposite p2)
    31	    (first : Measurement Outcome (S.ExpandedLocalSpace p1.side))
    32	    (second : Measurement Outcome (S.ExpandedLocalSpace p2.side)) :
    33	    (∑ answer : Outcome, ∑ other : Outcome,
    34	      if answer = other then 0 else DistanceCalculus.stateQForm S.psiHat
    35	        (S.place p1 (first.effect answer) * S.place p2 (second.effect other))) ≤ 1 := by
    36	  have h := DistanceCalculus.point_defect_eq
    37	    (S.placedMeasurement p1 first) (S.placedMeasurement p2 second) S.psiHat
    38	  simp only [ProjectiveSetting.placedMeasurement_effect, S.psiHat_norm, one_pow] at h
    39	  rw [h]
    40	  have hproduct (answer : Outcome) :
    41	      0 ≤ S.place p1 (first.effect answer) * S.place p2 (second.effect answer) := by
    42	    exact Commute.mul_nonneg
    43	      (S.place_nonneg p1 (first.pos answer))
    44	      (S.place_nonneg p2 (second.pos answer))
    45	      (S.place_comm p1 p2 hopp _ _)
    46	  have hdiag : 0 ≤ ∑ answer : Outcome, DistanceCalculus.stateQForm S.psiHat
    47	      (S.place p1 (first.effect answer) * S.place p2 (second.effect answer)) :=
    48	    Finset.sum_nonneg fun answer _ => DistanceCalculus.stateQForm_nonneg _
    49	      (hproduct answer)
    50	  linarith
    51

I’m finishing the repository-level checks now, including the required format for the new audit and the import/re-export placement of the new module.

    17	This file gives the common format and terminology for audit documents under

    21	
    22	## Metadata
    23	
    24	Every audit should begin with YAML front matter in this shape:
    25	
    26	```yaml
    27	---
    28	title: "Short human-readable title"
    29	date: YYYY-MM-DD
    30	purpose: >
    31	  One or two sentences explaining what the audit records and how it should be

    44	The values should be quoted strings such as `"#913"` so YAML parses them as
    45	text rather than comments.

    47	Existing or useful classification fields may be kept. In this repository the
    48	common ones are:

    51	status: active

    53	kind: naming-audit

    59	help later readers sort or review the audit.

    61	## File Names
    62	
    63	Dated audit artifacts should use a leading `YYYY-MM-DD_` filename. For example,

   106	| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
   107	| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |
   108	
   109	An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
   110	phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
   111	In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.
   112	
   113	File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
   114	named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
   115	exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.
   116	
   117	### Shared helpers
   118	
   119	When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
   120	more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
   121	shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
   122	ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
   123	call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.
   124	
   125	Procedure:
   126	
   127	1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   128	   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   129	   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   130	   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   131	   explicit argument.
   132	2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   133	   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   134	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   135	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   136	   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
   137	3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   138	   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
   139	4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   140	   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   141	   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   142	   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   143	   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   144	   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
   145	5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   146	   blueprint location it supports.
   147	
   148	### Legacy identifier treatment
   149	
   150	If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
   151	describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
   152	identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
   153	in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.
   154	
   155	Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
   156	public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
   157	shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
   158	blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.
   159	
   160	## Review Checklist
   161	
   162	Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
   163	documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.
   164	
   165	- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
   166	      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
   167	      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
   168	      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
   169	      implementation-phase labels)?
   170	- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
   171	      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
   172	      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
   173	      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
   174	      source does not use them that way?
   175	- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
   176	      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
   177	      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
   178	      that order of preference?
   179	- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
   180	      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
   181	      construction they support?
   182	- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
   183	      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
   184	      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
   185	- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
   186	      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
   187	      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
   188	      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
   189	- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
   190	      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
   191	      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
   192	      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.

\title{Documenting Possible Gaps, Counterexamples, and Formalization Deviations}
\author{}

\section{Purpose}

When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.

The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
lemma was applied.

The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
prose.

\section{Concision and Readability}

A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.

The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
derivation genuinely needs room.

Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.

If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
the issue or pull request in a footnote.

\section{When the Investigation Starts}

The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
argument.

The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
relevant files already compile.

At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
formalized.

A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
mathematics.

Once a cited statement is established to be mathematically false, the repair
and escalation procedure is governed by Section~6 of
\path{local/protocols/issues-prs.md}.  Before asking the human owner to choose a
replacement, a dedicated mathematical-gap session must produce a correction
which is correct, sufficient for every paper and blueprint use, and minimal,
then iterate it against the Lean statement and its downstream consumers.  A
Claude Fable~5.1 session is currently launched by the owner session through its
Agent tool; a Codex main session requests that lane on progress log~\#27 rather
than dispatching a Codex worker.  Only after the astra poller reports
availability on owner inbox~\#26 does the Codex route become
\texttt{dispatch.sh --role mathfix} with astra.  A change to a mathematical
definition or game is escalated immediately; other repairs reach the owner
inbox only after the shared convergence budget expires.

Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
implementation.

\section{When to Write a Note}

A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
relation.

A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.

Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.

When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
though it were the paper theorem.

This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
argument.

A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.

\section{Counterexamples}

If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.

When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.

\section{Revision of a Note}

A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
which point remains unsettled.

Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
discussion.

\section{Form of the Note}

Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant

Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
around the mathematical assertion and its proof.

The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.

Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.

Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.

Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
equations.

Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.

The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
footnotes.

The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,
that the matter is only notational, that an intermediate estimate needs a
harmless correction, that a hypothesis is missing, that there is a theorem-level
gap, or that the question remains open.  The classification should reflect the
mathematics, not the amount of formal work required.

\section{Decision Principle}

The formal development should not silently replace the cited assertion by a
different one.  If the formal statement differs from the cited source, the
reason for the difference should be written down.  Conversely, the note should
not overstate the conclusion.  A wrong intermediate scalar is not a fatal gap in
the theorem if the corrected scalar is bounded by the error parameter appearing
in the theorem statement.

   213	### Tracking issues
   214	
   215	Use the **Tracking Issue** template (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/tracking-issue.yml`).
   216	Label with `tracking`; add `chapter-tracking` for the long-lived chapter
   217	overview trackers. A tracking issue should begin by naming the mathematical
   218	objective and citing the paper or blueprint labels that the child issues cover.
   219	The `issue-automation` workflow will automatically:
   220	
   221	- Rely on GitHub's native sub-issue progress instead of editing body checkboxes.
   222	- Post progress comments on linked issues when PRs merge.
   223	- Suggest or create `follow-up` issues for genuine deferred work called out by merged PRs.
   224	
   225	The repository does not currently use a live `all-resolved` label, so do not
   226	add one manually.
   227	
   228	### Pinned issues
   229	
   230	The three most active tracking issues are pinned to the top of the Issues tab.
   231	Update pins when priorities shift (`gh issue pin/unpin`). GitHub allows at most
   232	3 pinned issues.
   233	
   234	### Milestones
   235	
   236	Use milestones to group issues targeting a shared deadline (e.g., a paper
   237	submission or a toolchain bump). Assign a milestone when the issue has a concrete
   238	target date; remove it when the date no longer applies.
   239	
   240	### Discussions
   241	
   242	GitHub Discussions is enabled for design questions, proof strategy debates, and
   243	topics that don't map to a single actionable issue. Use issues for concrete work
   244	items; use discussions for open-ended conversations.
   245	
   246	### Blueprint sync issues
   247	
   248	When the LaTeX blueprint is out of sync with Lean code, open an issue with
   249	the `blueprint-sync` label. Describe which chapter, theorem, or definition
   250	needs `\lean{}` / `\leanok` tags.
   251	
   252	Automated drift detection: the [blueprint ↔ Lean sync check][ci-sync] runs
   253	on every PR and fails when a `\leanok` tag sits on a Lean declaration whose
   254	transitive axiom closure still depends on `sorryAx`. See
   255	[`docs/ci-blueprint-sync.md`][ci-sync] for what it checks and how to run it
   256	locally.
   257	
   258	[ci-sync]: ci-blueprint-sync.md
   259	
   260	### Stale-issue audits
   261	
   262	Issues that cite specific `sorry` sites, file/line locations, or declaration
   263	names drift out of date as `main` moves. Keep those citations precise rather
   264	than replacing them with vague prose: update paths, line numbers, theorem labels,
   265	and short source paraphrases when the source moves. Before starting a new
   266	proof-closing round (or periodically as maintenance), run the audit script to
   267	list open issues whose citations no longer resolve:
   268	
   269	```bash
   270	gh issue list --repo LionSR/MIPStarRE --state open --limit 500 \
   271	  --json number,title,body,url,labels > /tmp/open-issues.json
   272	python3 scripts/audit_stale_issues.py --issues /tmp/open-issues.json
   273	```
   274	
   275	The tool is report-only. Human review decides which flags warrant closing
   276	the issue, updating its body, or dismissing as a false positive. A weekly
   277	read-only GitHub Actions wrapper runs the same export-and-audit sequence and
   278	uploads an artifact only when citations are flagged. See
   279	[`docs/stale_issue_audit.md`](stale_issue_audit.md) for the full workflow.

   368	## 5. Review Checklist
   369	
   370	Every PR touching Lean code should be reviewed against these criteria:
   371	
   372	1. **Proof correctness** -- No unexplained `sorry`. No `axiom` unless discussed.
   373	   Run `rg -n "sorry|axiom" <file>` to verify.
   374	
   375	2. **Mathlib style** -- Follow the lean-conventions `MATHLIB_naming` and
   376	   `MATHLIB_doc` references. See the lean-conventions `MATHLIB_pr-review`
   377	   reference for the full Mathlib review guide.
   378	
   379	3. **Paper terminology** -- Public Lean names, module docstrings, declaration
   380	   docstrings, and documentation-visible comments should use terminology from
   381	   the paper and blueprint, not implementation history. See
   382	   [mathematical_language.md](mathematical_language.md) for the project-local
   383	   language rule for Lean documentation and public names. Reviewers should flag
   384	   names that encode historical formalization status rather than mathematical
   385	   content. When an old public identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR,
   386	   record the required migration in the issue, PR description, or an audit file
   387	   under [audits/](../audits/).
   388	   New and substantively updated audit files should follow the term norm and
   389	   format in
   390	   [audits/2026-04-29_audit-document-format.md](../audits/2026-04-29_audit-document-format.md).
   391	   Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
   392	   public name.
   393	   Review-fix PRs must read the relevant audit files under [audits/](../audits/)
   394	   before changing names or prose. If an audit marks a naming migration or
   395	   historical-formalization term as in scope for the fix, addressing it or
   396	   explicitly updating the audit trail is a merge blocker.
   397	
   398	4. **Linter hygiene** -- Linter-warning cleanup must fix warnings, not mask
   399	   them with broad `set_option linter.<name> false` blocks. See
   400	   [project_conventions.md](project_conventions.md#linter-warnings) for the project rule and the narrow
   401	   exception policy.
   402	
   403	5. **Type safety** -- No universe mismatches, coercion problems, or unresolved
   404	   metavariables.
   405	
   406	6. **Performance** -- Avoid expensive tactics on large types (e.g., `decide` on
   407	   `Fin 1000`). Watch for timeout-prone proof terms.
   408	
   409	7. **Modularity** -- Are new lemmas general enough to be reused? Could any be
   410	   upstreamed to Mathlib?
   411	
   412	8. **Documentation** -- Every new `def` and major `theorem` must have a docstring.
   413	   Module files should have a header comment with `## References` citing the
   414	   relevant arXiv paper(s).
   415	
   416	9. **Blueprint sync and paper origin** -- If the PR formalizes a statement
   417	   from the blueprint, add `\lean{LeanDeclName}` and `\leanok` tags to the
   418	   corresponding `blueprint/src/chapter/*.tex` file. If the PR adds a public
   419	   auxiliary lemma that is not a named statement in the original paper, record
   420	   that explicitly: the Lean docstring should call it a formalization-only
   421	   auxiliary lemma and the blueprint should either omit it as private/internal
   422	   infrastructure or include it as a clearly subordinate support node connected
   423	   by `\uses{...}`. See
   424	   [blueprint_style_guide.md](blueprint_style_guide.md#recording-formalization-only-lemmas).
   425	   PR descriptions and follow-up issues should cite the corresponding paper or
   426	   blueprint path, line, label, and a short quotation or precise paraphrase.
   427	   Reviewers should also check for early drift from the source: new hypotheses,
   428	   weakened conclusions, changed quantifier order, altered error parameters,
   429	   or renamed obligation structures that turn a paper theorem into a conditional
   430	   theorem.  If such drift appears, request a statement integrity audit before
   431	   reviewing the proof.  A bridge or residual hypothesis should be treated as
   432	   proof debt to remove, not as evidence that the paper statement has been
   433	   formalized.
   434	
   435	10. **Scaffolding integrity** -- If the PR introduces or modifies scaffolded
   436	   definitions (types, theorem statements with `sorry` proofs), verify that
   437	   the types and API surface align with Mathlib. Scaffolding that uses custom
   438	   types incompatible with Mathlib blocks future proof work. See
   439	   the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference and
   440	   [project_conventions.md](project_conventions.md) for details.
   441	
   442	11. **Proof-evasion anti-patterns** -- Review against
   443	   [anti_patterns.md](anti_patterns.md), which catalogues subtler failure
   444	   modes that pass the proof-integrity blocker checks but still fail
   445	   to prove the claimed mathematics: conclusion-shaped hypotheses (A1),
   446	   `:= rfl` definitional sleight-of-hand (A2), zero-fallback branches
   447	   hiding preconditions (A3), trivial default witnesses (A4),
   448	   Mathlib-bypass castles (A5), and external `*Statement` smuggles (A6).
   449	   Use the reviewer checklist at the end of that file.
   450	
   451	12. **Proof frontier integrity** -- If the PR introduces or threads structure
   452	   fields such as `*Input`, `*Residual`, `*BridgeInputs`, `*Witness`,
   453	   `*Statement`, `*Conclusion`, or `*Package`, review it against
   454	   [proof_frontier_review.md](proof_frontier_review.md). A PR that only
   455	   repackages an assumption should not be described as proving the corresponding
   456	   paper step; it must name the missing obligation discharger or link the native
   457	   sub-issue that tracks it.  For source-labelled theorems, the preferred repair
   458	   is to extract any usable proof content into source-faithful lemmas and
   459	   restore the paper-aligned statement, even if the remaining proof is a tracked
   460	   `sorry` during the cleanup.  For source-labelled proof gaps, also use the
   461	   protocol in
   462	   [paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex](paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex).
   463	
   464	### Semantic scaffold checklist (required for core math objects)
   465	
   466	For semantic objects such as measurements, submeasurements, distributions,
   467	averaged operators, and packaged theorem outputs, reviewers should additionally
   468	verify:
   469	
   470	1. **Impossible states check** -- Does the structure exclude states that are
   471	   impossible under the paper definition?
   472	2. **Derived-field check** -- If a field is mathematically derived
   473	   (e.g. `total = ∑ a, outcome a`), is it either derived on demand or stored
   474	   together with an equality proof (e.g. `sum_eq_total`)?
   475	3. **Invariant bundling check** -- Are core invariants (positivity,
   476	   boundedness/normalization, completeness where applicable) encoded directly
   477	   in the structure or constructor, rather than deferred to downstream lemmas?
   478	4. **Stress-test check** -- Is at least one nontrivial theorem in scope of the
   479	   PR provable/stated against the scaffold without adding ad hoc assumptions?
   480	
   481	If any answer is "no", treat the scaffold as unsafe and request a follow-up
   482	before broad theorem layering continues.

    27	/-- Coefficient lists for a univariate polynomial of degree at most `c` in the
    28	direct scalar field. -/
    29	abbrev DirectDegPoly (D : DirectLdParams) (c : ℕ) :=
    30	  Fin (c + 1) → DirectScalarQ D
    31	
    32	/-- A direct line polynomial evaluates to `a` at `u` when `u` lies on the line
    33	and every parameter presenting `u` gives value `a`.  The universal clause
    34	keeps the zero-direction case explicit. -/
    35	def DirectEvaluatesTo {D : DirectLdParams} {c : ℕ} (line : DirectLineDesc D)
    36	    (f : DirectDegPoly D c) (u : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)
    37	    (a : DirectScalarQ D) : Prop :=
    38	  (∃ t : DirectScalarQ D, u = line.base + t • line.direction) ∧
    39	    ∀ t : DirectScalarQ D, u = line.base + t • line.direction →
    40	      evalCoefficient f t = a
    41	
    42	/-- Option-completed evaluation of a direct line polynomial.  `none` is an
    43	explicit outcome when the point does not determine an evaluation; no field
    44	value is used as a fallback. -/
    45	noncomputable def directEvalOpt {D : DirectLdParams} {c : ℕ}
    46	    (line : DirectLineDesc D) (u : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)
    47	    (f : DirectDegPoly D c) : Option (DirectScalarQ D) := by
    48	  classical
    49	  exact if h : ∃ a : DirectScalarQ D, DirectEvaluatesTo line f u a then
    50	    some (Classical.choose h)
    51	  else none

    36	/-- Successful completed evaluation means evaluation at every parameter
    37	presenting the point, including when the line direction is zero. -/
    38	theorem directEvalOpt_eq_some_iff {params : DirectLdParams} {degree : ℕ}
    39	    (line : DirectLineDesc params) (point : Fin params.m → DirectScalarQ params)
    40	    (coeffs : DirectDegPoly params degree) (answer : DirectScalarQ params) :
    41	    directEvalOpt line point coeffs = some answer ↔
    42	      DirectEvaluatesTo line coeffs point answer := by
    43	  classical
    44	  unfold directEvalOpt

    46	  · simp only [Option.some.injEq]

    50	    · intro heval

    52	      exact ((Classical.choose_spec hexists).2 parameter hparameter).symm.trans

    55	    exact fun heval => hexists ⟨answer, heval⟩

     3	/-!
     4	# Collision bounds for direct line coefficients
     5	
     6	This module bounds the probability that two distinct coefficient vectors give
     7	the same value at a uniformly sampled affine parameter.  It uses the existing
     8	coefficient-polynomial representation and Mathlib's univariate root count.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	- `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:331-344`
    13	- `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1595-1603`
    14	-/
    15	
    16	open scoped BigOperators
    17	
    18	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    19	
    20	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    21	open MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries
    22	
    23	noncomputable section
    24	
    25	/-- Two distinct direct coefficient vectors of degree at most `degree` agree
    26	at a uniformly sampled parameter with probability at most `degree / q`.
    27	
    28	This is a Lean-only auxiliary. The cited paper passages describe the coefficient
    29	answer format and apply Schwartz-Zippel to a later multivariate collision term;
    30	they do not state this exact univariate averaging bound.
    31	
    32	The estimate has no hypothesis `degree < q`; when the displayed bound exceeds
    33	one it remains a valid, deliberately nontruncated root-count bound. -/
    34	theorem directCoefficientCollision_avg_le (D : DirectLdParams) (degree : ℕ)
    35	    (a b : DirectDegPoly D degree) (hne : a ≠ b) :
    36	    avgOver (uniformDistribution (DirectScalarQ D))
    37	        (fun t => if evalCoefficient a t = evalCoefficient b t then
